# Code review iteration

Reviewed the whole `github.com/kamilsk/retry/v5` module at commit `0f199af 2021-02-23`: root package (retry.go, context.go, errors.go), the backoff, jitter, and strategy packages, the sandbox and examples sub-modules, tests, Makefile, .golangci.yml, .travis.yml, and README.md. Review angle: semantic correctness of retry/backoff/context handling, goroutine and error-propagation guarantees for a public library with real users, and how the 2021-era decisions hold up against Go 1.26-era idioms and tooling. `.github/issues/` and `.github/roadmap/` were excluded as offline backlog dumps. `.github/reviews/` did not exist before this iteration, so there are no previous review files to match against; all findings below are new.

Severity: **Crit** / **High** / **Med** / **Low** / **Nit**.
Class: `correctness` · `security` · `concurrency` · `perf` · `api` · `idiom` · `modern` · `test` · `build` · `docs`.

## 1. Unwrap discards the error chain and strategies see nil

Anchor: errors.go:14-29, consumed at retry.go:47.

```go
func unwrap(err error) error {
	for err != nil {
		layer, is := err.(wrapper)
		if is {
			err = layer.Unwrap()
			continue
		}
		...
	}
	return err
}
```

The loop follows `Unwrap()`/`Cause()` until `err == nil` and then returns whatever it ended on — including nil. Any chain that terminates in a type whose `Unwrap` returns nil makes `unwrap` return **nil instead of the last real error**. The library's own `Error` type is such a type (`Unwrap() error { return nil }`, errors.go:12), so `unwrap(Error("boom")) == nil`, and with the repo's own test fixture `unwrap(layer{causer{Error("failure")}})` walks layer → causer → Error → nil.

`Do` feeds `core = unwrap(err)` to every strategy (retry.go:47-49). So after a genuinely failed attempt, an error-inspecting strategy — `sandbox.CheckError`, the flagship error-classification feature — receives nil, takes its `err == nil` early-return (sandbox/strategy.go:39), and answers "retry", even for permanent, explicitly non-retriable errors. Retry policies based on the error are silently inert for a wide class of real-world errors (any custom error type implementing `Unwrap() error` that returns nil at the root). The test suite never catches this because no test asserts what strategies receive (see [[#12. Tests never observe the error passed to strategies]]), and `TestUnwrap` uses `errors.New` as the root, which has no `Unwrap` method.

Note the intended "strategies see nil before the first attempt" behavior only works by accident of this bug: `err` starts as the `internal` sentinel, which unwraps to nil.

**Fix.** Keep the last non-nil error: compute `next` from `Unwrap`/`Cause` and `return err` when `next == nil`. Make attempt-zero explicit in `Do` (pass nil while `attempt == 0` or while `err == internal`) instead of relying on the sentinel unwrapping to nothing. Better yet, drop pre-unwrapping entirely and pass the error as-is — since Go 1.13 `errors.Is`/`errors.As` traverse chains themselves, and pre-flattening to the root actively hides intermediate wrapper types from `errors.As`. While here, delete `Error.Unwrap` (an always-nil `Unwrap` is noise) and consider dropping the `Cause()` shim — github.com/pkg/errors has been archived since 2021.

## 2. Toolchain, CI, and lint stack are five years stale

Anchor: go.mod:3, .travis.yml:1-23, .golangci.yml:10-26, Makefile:5.

The repo effectively has no working infrastructure today:

- `go 1.11` directive (go.mod:3; examples go 1.13, sandbox go 1.11). The current era is Go 1.26; everything from `errors.Join` to `math/rand/v2`, `//go:build`, and loopvar semantics postdates this module's floor.
- Travis CI (.travis.yml) is dead for OSS — travis-ci.com ended free open-source builds in 2021, so no CI has run since; the build matrix (1.11–1.16, Makefile GO_VERSIONS too) is entirely EOL, and the README build badge is dark.
- .golangci.yml enables linters that were removed from golangci-lint years ago (`deadcode`, `structcheck`, `varcheck` removed in v1.49, 2022; `exportloopref` obsolete since Go 1.22 made loop variables per-iteration), and the file predates the golangci-lint v2 config schema.
- No GitHub Actions, no Dependabot/Renovate, no `govulncheck`, no CodeQL.
- Legacy `// +build go1.13` constraint (sandbox/example_test.go:1) instead of `//go:build`; `math/rand` where `math/rand/v2` is now standard (jitter package).
- README badge/link rot: rawgit.com (awesome badge) shut down in 2019, Travis and Code Climate badges point at dead pipelines; examples/sandbox modules still pin `v5.0.0-rc8` via replace.

**Fix.** One modernization pass: (1) bump `go` directive to a supported floor (e.g. 1.25) and run `gofmt`/`go fix` over the tree; (2) replace Travis with a GitHub Actions workflow testing `stable` + `oldstable` with `-race`, plus `govulncheck` and golangci-lint v2 jobs, and add Dependabot for gomod + actions; (3) regenerate .golangci.yml against the v2 schema with today's linter set (`errorlint` and `copyloopvar` would both have flagged real issues in this review); (4) migrate jitter to `math/rand/v2` (API break — fold into the next major, see [[#6. Shared rand generators race under concurrent retries]]); (5) refresh README badges and finish or cut the placeholder sections; (6) release a final v5 so examples/sandbox stop pinning an rc.

## 3. Go can report cancellation for an action that already succeeded

Anchor: retry.go:93-98.

```go
select {
case <-breaker.Done():
	return breaker.Err()
case err := <-done:
	return err
}
```

When both channels are ready, Go's runtime picks a case uniformly at random. If the action completes at roughly the same moment the deadline fires — the common case being an action that barely beats its timeout — `done` already holds `nil` (success), yet `Go` may return `context.DeadlineExceeded`. The caller then believes the operation failed and may re-execute a non-idempotent action that in fact committed. Symmetrically, a meaningful last error can be replaced by a bare `context.Canceled`. `Do` does not have this flaw: its loop checks success before consulting the breaker, so success deterministically wins there. `Go` should offer the same guarantee.

**Fix.** Prefer a delivered result over the cancellation signal:

```go
select {
case err := <-done:
	return err
case <-breaker.Done():
	select {
	case err := <-done:
		return err
	default:
	}
	return breaker.Err()
}
```

A result that arrives after `Go` returns is still abandoned — that is inherent to the fire-and-forget design and worth documenting explicitly — but a result that has already been delivered must never be discarded.

## 4. Backoff overflow yields negative delays and jitter panics

Anchor: backoff.go:39-43 and 55-67; jitter.go:22, 34, 48; timer at strategy/strategy.go:94.

```go
func Exponential(factor time.Duration, base float64) Algorithm {
	return func(attempt uint) time.Duration {
		return factor * time.Duration(math.Pow(base, float64(attempt)))
	}
}
```

`attempt` is unbounded: without a `Limit` strategy, `Do` loops until success, so long outages produce large attempt numbers. `Exponential(100*time.Millisecond, 2)` overflows int64 nanoseconds around attempt 37; the float-to-int conversion of an out-of-range value is implementation-defined and the multiplication wraps, producing negative durations. `time.NewTimer` with a negative duration fires immediately, so exactly when a dependency is down long enough to matter, the backoff silently degrades into a zero-delay hot loop hammering it — the opposite of its purpose. `Fibonacci` wraps the same way via uint arithmetic (backoff.go:59-63).

It gets worse with jitter: `jitter.Full` and `jitter.Equal` call `generator.Int63n(int64(duration))`, which **panics** for any duration ≤ 0 (overflowed exponential, or simply `Constant(0)`); `Deviation` panics when its computed `max == min` (e.g. `factor == 0`). Inside `Do` there is no recover, so the panic propagates straight into the caller's goroutine and crashes the process.

**Fix.** Saturate instead of wrapping: cap the exponent (bit-shift with a ceiling rather than `math.Pow`) and clamp all algorithm outputs to a non-negative range, and guard the transformations (`if duration <= 0 { return 0 }`). Consider exposing an explicit max-delay knob — every mainstream retry library (cenkalti/backoff, AWS SDK) has one, and it is the natural place for the clamp.

## 5. NetworkError misses wrapped errors and uses deprecated Temporary

Anchor: sandbox/strategy.go:57-64.

```go
func NetworkError(defaults bool) func(error) bool {
	return func(err error) bool {
		if err, is := err.(net.Error); is {
			return err.Temporary() || err.Timeout()
		}
		return defaults
	}
}
```

Two problems. First, the plain type assertion only matches the exact value it is handed; anything wrapped with `fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)` at an intermediate layer is invisible (and today, because of [[#1. Unwrap discards the error chain and strategies see nil]], the handler frequently receives nil and is skipped entirely). `errors.As` is the correct tool. Second, `net.Error.Temporary` has been deprecated since Go 1.18 because its meaning was never well-defined — it famously classified `ECONNRESET` as temporary while treating semantically identical failures differently — and staticcheck flags it (SA1019). This is the package's core error-classification primitive, so misclassification directly translates into wrong retry decisions.

Related: sandbox is a separate, never-tagged module (`github.com/kamilsk/retry/sandbox`, sandbox/go.mod:1) pinned to `v5.0.0-rc8` through a `replace` — consumers cannot actually depend on it in any sane way.

**Fix.** Use `var netErr net.Error; errors.As(err, &netErr)`, and base the retriable decision on `Timeout()`, `errors.Is(err, os.ErrDeadlineExceeded)`, and explicit syscall errno checks instead of `Temporary()`. Then decide the sandbox module's fate: error classification is arguably the most requested retry feature, so graduate `CheckError` into the versioned module proper — or delete the sandbox to stop shipping unversionable code.

## 6. Shared rand generators race under concurrent retries

Anchor: jitter.go:20, 32, 44, 57.

All four transformations capture a caller-supplied `*rand.Rand`, which is documented as not safe for concurrent use. The natural usage pattern — build one `how := retry.How{...}` with a jitter strategy and reuse it across requests/goroutines, exactly what the README (README.md:27-36) and sandbox example demonstrate — means concurrent `Do`/`Go` calls invoke the same generator simultaneously: a data race (`-race` flags it) that can corrupt generator state. Nothing in the docs warns about this, and the API shape actively invites it.

**Fix.** Accept a nil generator and fall back to `math/rand/v2` top-level functions, which are goroutine-safe and auto-seeded (this also retires the `rand.NewSource(time.Now().UnixNano())` boilerplate the README teaches); alternatively guard the captured generator with a mutex. Either way, document the concurrency contract of a Transformation. The signature change is a good candidate for the same major-version pass as [[#2. Toolchain, CI, and lint stack are five years stale]].

## 7. Zero-attempt sentinel error is unexported and unmatchable

Anchor: errors.go:3, escaping at retry.go:42 and 64.

```go
const internal Error = "have no any try"
```

Whenever strategies deny the very first attempt (e.g. `strategy.Limit(0)`), `Do` and `Go` return this sentinel to the caller — the test suite even pins it (`expected{0, Error("have no any try")}`, retry_test.go:162). It is observable public behavior implemented as an unexported constant: callers cannot `errors.Is` against it and are reduced to matching the string `"have no any try"`, which is also broken English on the public surface of the library.

**Fix.** Export it — `var ErrNoAttempts = Error("no attempts were made")` (or similar) — return it from both entry points, document it on `Do`/`Go`, and keep the old string only if you believe someone is matching on it today. This is exactly what `errors.Is` sentinels are for.

## 8. README quick-start example does not compile

Anchor: README.md:27-36; also 53 and 69.

```go
how := []retry.How{
	strategy.Limit(5),
	...
}
```

`retry.How` is already a slice (`type How = []func(Breaker, uint, error) bool`, retry.go:29), so `[]retry.How` declares a slice of slices; `strategy.Limit(5)` is not assignable to its element type, and the subsequent `retry.Do(ctx, action, how...)` fails as well. The closure above it also references undeclared `req` and `resp`. This is the first code a prospective user copies, and it fails at the compiler. Further down, the "How to" section has literally said `rewriting...` and "Outcomes" has been an ellipsis since the v5 release in 2020 — for five years the front page has told users the docs are unfinished.

**Fix.** Change to `how := retry.How{...}` and make the snippet a complete, compiling program (sandbox/example_test.go is 90% of it already). Better: keep README snippets as testable `Example` functions in the repo so the compiler guards the docs, and finish or delete the placeholder sections.

## 9. Interruption discards the last action error

Anchor: retry.go:52-54 (and the same choice at retry.go:94-95).

When the breaker fires, `Do` returns `breaker.Err()` — a bare `context.Canceled`/`context.DeadlineExceeded` — and throws away the error from the last attempt. For diagnostics and alerting, "deadline exceeded after 4 attempts, last error: 503 from upstream" is materially more useful than "context deadline exceeded", and today callers have no way to recover the cause. In 2021 there was no good way to return both; since Go 1.20 there is.

**Fix.** Return `errors.Join(breaker.Err(), lastErr)` (or wrap with `%w` around the cancellation error) so both `errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded)` and the last cause survive; take care not to join the internal zero-attempt sentinel. This changes observable behavior for callers comparing errors with `==`, so ship it behind the next minor with a release note — or fold it into the v6 pass.

## 10. Do and Go give inconsistent panic guarantees

Anchor: retry.go:79-91.

`Go` recovers a panicking action and flattens it into an ordinary error return — losing the stack trace entirely, since `fmt.Errorf("retry: unexpected panic: %#v", r)` captures only the value — while `Do` lets the identical panic tear down the caller's goroutine (see the jitter panic in [[#4. Backoff overflow yields negative delays and jitter panics]] for a concrete in-library trigger). Two entry points, silently different contracts, and neither documents it. Disguising a panic as a returned error also means a caller's blanket error handling can mask a genuine bug indefinitely.

**Fix.** Pick one contract and apply it to both. The current ecosystem consensus (e.g. `x/sync/errgroup`, which now repropagates goroutine panics wrapped in a `PanicError` carrying the stack) is to either repanic on the caller's goroutine or return a dedicated exported error type that embeds `debug.Stack()` output. Either beats a `%#v` of the panic value; document whichever you choose on both `Do` and `Go`.

## 11. Alias-based API triples the Breaker interface

Anchor: retry.go:9, 14, 29; duplicated at strategy/strategy.go:9 and sandbox/strategy.go:13.

The public API is built entirely on type aliases — `Action`, `How`, `Breaker = interface {...}`, `strategy.Strategy` — so that structurally identical anonymous types interchange across packages without imports. The cost: the `Breaker` interface literal is copy-pasted verbatim in three packages, exported signatures must spell out `strategies ...func(Breaker, uint, error) bool` in full (retry.go:38), and pkg.go.dev renders aliases as second-class citizens with no place to hang methods or docs. The cycle the aliases were presumably avoiding does not exist: strategy imports nothing from retry, so retry could simply import strategy.

**Fix.** In the next major, make them defined types (`type Strategy func(Breaker, uint, error) bool` in one place, `type How []Strategy`) and have `retry.Do` accept `...strategy.Strategy`. Func literals remain assignable to defined func types, so ergonomics for callers are unchanged; only pre-declared variables of user-defined func types would need an explicit conversion, which is rare.

## 12. Tests never observe the error passed to strategies

Anchor: retry_test.go:135-164; strategy/strategy_test.go:85-128; examples/http_test.go:1; Makefile:76.

The `Do`/`Go` table tests assert attempt counts and the returned error, but no test ever asserts the `err` argument a strategy receives during the loop — precisely the seam where [[#1. Unwrap discards the error chain and strategies see nil]] lives, which is why a High-severity semantic bug survives a green suite. Meanwhile the strategy tests assert wall-clock deltas with one-millisecond tolerances (`time.Since(past) < time.Millisecond`) that are flaky on loaded CI runners; `examples/http_test.go` is a one-line empty stub committed as "rewriting"; and the Makefile's 1-second test timeout (Makefile:76, `TIMEOUT ?= 1s`) leaves no headroom for `-race` on slow machines.

**Fix.** Add a spy strategy to the `Do`/`Go` tables that records the errors it is called with and assert against the action's actual returns — a five-line helper that would have caught the unwrap bug. Replace timing assertions with generous bounds or an injected clock, implement or delete the http example, and raise the default test timeout.
